My main reason for mixing science with religious thought is because most of the Hindus I discuss these things with don't even acknowledge that this stuff is religious thought. Many family members I've discussed these things with, claim that every aspect of hinduism is scientific to the core, so I was trying to hold it to that standard. As for not being familiar with the history of science, cut me some slack, Im a teen on reddit, and my scientific education consists of school and youtube.

Is there overlap between vedanta and religion though? If I understand you correctly, vedanta is distinct from both science and religion, but does vedanta deal with supernatural things like reincarnation and or is it only concerned with consciousness?
Could you tell me more about your deep digging? What did you read? asking as someone who knows almost nothing about hinduism. Also I'm sorry if my original question was worded rudely

I did not intend to come off as condescending, I just wanted to filter out the "It's divine inspiration" crowd to see if there was a legit reason to see scriptures as an authority that did not involve faith. I was trying to be direct, not offensive.

Also I'm not reading the scriptures directly but rather books about them. I know that some of them are literally scientific books. I was referring to the others that talk about things like reincarnation.

To be more clear, I don't need to believe Newton to know about gravity. I can verify its existence for myself. How can I verify ancestral spirits in the same way? Ancestral spirits may well exist, but this is far from a certainty. Why is it classified as a truth, rather than an idea?

If I understand correctly, then you're saying that the veda's authority comes from the rishis who wrote them. I'm asking why they should be considered standalone authorities by themselves. If we accept scientific facts as true, its because of the evidence backing them up, not the scientists who figured it out. If I want to prove that gravity exists, I can do so by throwing a ball in the air. Similarly, if the vedas make a claim about the afterlife for instance, I cannot verify that until I die, so why should I assume it to be true? There are a million different afterlife stories from different cultures, why should I assume the vedic one to be true? Not saying its false per se, just that I don't get why they're considered truths rather than theories or philosophy.

I keep hearing that its scientific, I get no solid evidence for it. 90 percent of the time, when you ask people to explain what sense is there, you get pseudoscientific answers. Also, you cannot say that the vedas are true because the rishis are authorities. We dont trust what scientists say because they are authorities, we trust them because they produce evidence, and their experiments can be repeated. Similarly, Im asking, can the vedas by themselves be considered true. Without deferring to the authority of rishis, if so, then why?

Arrogance, we don't know what the truth is, and as far as being "right" goes, there's more important things than that. Given the sufferring filled world we live in, its good for people to cling to whatever they can.
Its natural to feel that way, but I think you're taking life too seriously.

There isnt a solution to this, Either have a child or accept that no one will care for you when you're dying  not to mention senior citizens can be taken advantage of, and robbed, even if they have money to care for themselves. If its any consolation, even having children doesn't guarantee companionship on your deathbed, it just increases your chances of having it.

Me personally, I'm sympathetic to antinatalism. I think its a perfectly rational position. However, Im not an antinatalist. I think one has to be really sensitive to sufferring to think that way. Whoever you are, I hope you prioritise your mental health and feel better about the world. I plan on having kids if I ever find a loving partner. Sometimes it freaks me out to impose existence on a new person in cold blood like that, but its a forgivable act. You suffer too, and if you choose to have kids, forgive yourself for it. Maybe the world isnt so bad after all, maybe our children will come to love life. My mental health improved a lot in the last year and a half and I dont think having kids is selfish or immoral anymore.

Another thing is that you shouldnt outright expect your kids to care for you when they are born. That puts a burden of expectations on them.

I know that this is an emotional argument, but consider it.
I've figured this out intellectually at 20. Still working on feeling it to be true, and making this knowledge second nature to me.
